title: Coffee shop seats and revenue: reading regression output

stimulus.title: Seats and weekly revenue at 15 coffee shops
stimulus.text: A coffee chain records the number of seats and the weekly revenue (thousands of dollars) at 15 of its shops. The scatterplot and part of the regression output are below. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of 15 coffee shops: seats from 12 to 50 against weekly revenue from 8.1 to 19.8 thousand dollars, rising in a narrow straight band

table.caption: Regression of weekly revenue (thousands of dollars) on number of seats

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between number of seats and weekly revenue shown in the scatterplot.

rubric.point: Direction and form: a positive, linear association.
accept: shops with more seats tend to have higher revenue, in a straight-line pattern

rubric.point: Strength and context: strong, with no clear outliers, describing seats and weekly revenue for these shops.
accept: strong association between seats and revenue, unusual points addressed

parts.sample: There is a strong, positive, linear association between the number of seats and weekly revenue for these 15 shops, with no clear outliers. Shops with more seats tend to have higher weekly revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining any variables you use, and interpret its slope in context.

rubric.point: Equation with variables defined: predicted revenue = 4.102 + 0.3121(seats), with revenue in thousands of dollars.
accept: y-hat = 4.102 + 0.3121x with y = weekly revenue (thousands of dollars) and x = number of seats

rubric.point: Slope: for each additional seat, the predicted weekly revenue increases by about 0.312 thousand dollars (about 312 dollars).
accept: the slope interpreted with "predicted" and both variables in context

parts.sample:
predicted revenue = 4.102 + 0.3121(seats), where revenue is weekly revenue in thousands of dollars and seats is the number of seats.
For each additional seat, the predicted weekly revenue increases by about 0.312 thousand dollars, about 312 dollars.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: One shop has 30 seats and weekly revenue of 15.1 thousand dollars. Calculate and interpret its residual.

rubric.point: Correct residual with work: predicted = 4.102 + 0.3121(30) = 13.47, so residual = 15.1 - 13.47 = 1.63.
Interpretation: the shop's weekly revenue is about 1.63 thousand dollars higher than the line predicts for a shop with 30 seats.
accept: positive residual interpreted as above the predicted revenue, in context

parts.sample:
predicted = 4.102 + 0.3121(30) = 13.47
residual = actual - predicted = 15.1 - 13.47 = 1.63
This shop's weekly revenue is about 1.63 thousand dollars (about 1,635 dollars) more than the line predicts for a shop with 30 seats.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Interpret the values of R-Sq and S in context.

rubric.point: R-Sq: about 96.3% of the variation in weekly revenue is accounted for by the linear model using number of seats.
accept: r^2 interpreted as variation in revenue explained by the line with seats

rubric.point: S: the actual weekly revenue of a shop typically differs from its predicted revenue by about 0.726 thousand dollars.
accept: s interpreted as a typical prediction error in thousands of dollars

parts.sample:
About 96.3% of the variation in weekly revenue is accounted for by the linear model using number of seats.
The actual weekly revenue of these shops typically differs from the revenue predicted by the line by about 0.726 thousand dollars, about 726 dollars.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The chain is planning a shop with 85 seats. Explain why using the line to predict its weekly revenue could be unreliable.

rubric.point: Identifies extrapolation: 85 seats is far outside the 12 to 50 seats in the data, so the linear pattern may not continue.
accept: the prediction is outside the range of the data

parts.sample: Predicting for 85 seats is extrapolation. The shops in the data have 12 to 50 seats, so nothing in the data shows that revenue keeps rising at the same rate for a shop that large.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Suppose a 16th shop with 85 seats and weekly revenue of 21.0 thousand dollars were added to the data. Explain how this point would affect the least-squares slope, and identify what kind of point it is.

rubric.point: Identifies the point as high leverage (its x value is far from the others) and influential, and explains that it lies far below the line (the line predicts about 30.6), so it would pull the line down at the right and make the slope smaller (about 0.206 instead of 0.312).
accept: a high-leverage, influential point that would decrease the slope because it sits well below the extended line

parts.sample: The point is a high-leverage point, because 85 seats is far from the other shops' 12 to 50 seats. The line predicts about 30.6 thousand dollars for 85 seats, but the shop earns only 21.0, so the point lies far below the line. Least squares would pull the line toward it, flattening the line: the slope would drop from about 0.312 to about 0.206. Because removing it would change the slope that much, it is an influential point.
